passage: I'm Maria. I've lived across from Simran's family in this old part of Ahmedabad for twenty years. This winter I kept seeing her, nine or ten years old, sitting on the steps of the stepwell near our lane with a notebook. Every evening she'd stop the elderly men playing cards and ask them things. Once I heard her say, 'But who built it? Was it a queen?' One uncle told her a long story about a queen who built it so travellers would never go thirsty. Simran wrote fast, tongue poking out. Later she knocked on my door to ask what I remembered of the well when it still had water. I don't know what drew her there. But she looked happy doing it.

qa.q: Where did Maria keep seeing Simran sit in the evenings?
qa.a: On the steps of the stepwell near their lane, with a notebook.

qa.q: What does Simran writing fast with her tongue poking out suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests she was absorbed and curious about the story, though Maria can't be sure what drew her.

qa.q: How could Simran's teacher support her interest in local history?
qa.a: The teacher could invite her to share the stories with the class and help her compare them with a library book about the city.

qa.q: How might the elderly card players feel about Simran's questions?
qa.a: They might enjoy being asked, glad that a child cares about the old stories they carry.

grounding: An observer sees a child gathering local history and a legend about her area from elders.

passage: Monday: In the Hindi period, Avni, ten, yawned through the Ramayana chapter. 'Old stories,' she whispered to Kashish. 'Nothing to do with us.' Thursday: At Kashish's house, her grandmother told them about the little squirrel who rolled in sand and shook it onto the stones while the monkeys built the great bridge. 'Such a tiny thing,' said Nani, 'and Ram stroked her back with thanks.' Avni sat very still. 'So even small help counts?' she asked. Next Monday: When class was cleaning the garden, Avni saw the youngest girl carrying just one pot. Kashish laughed. Avni said, 'Squirrel help. It counts.' The girl beamed. Avni asked the teacher for the next chapter.

qa.q: What did the squirrel do while the bridge was being built?
qa.a: She rolled in sand and shook it onto the stones.

qa.q: What was Avni thinking when she 'sat very still' listening to Nani?
qa.a: She was realising the old story had a meaning for her own life, that even small help matters.

qa.q: How did Avni use the story's moral in real life?
qa.a: She defended the youngest girl carrying one pot, saying small help counts, instead of laughing.

qa.q: How might the youngest girl have felt when Avni spoke up?
qa.a: She likely felt valued and proud that her small effort was noticed. 😊

grounding: Shows a child coming to see the moral of an epic story and applying it.

passage: Indu's eleventh birthday party was at seven, and she had invited her whole class, but the evening went wrong the moment Payal said on the phone, 'Sorry, I can't eat after sunset. It's Paryushan. My family is fasting this week.' Indu stared at the cake box. 'But the cake!' She almost said, 'Just once won't matter.' Then she remembered how much Payal knew about Christmas, and how she'd asked about the crib in Indu's house without laughing. There was only an hour before sunset. Indu ran to Mamma. 'Can we cut the cake early, at six, for anyone who comes?' Mamma nodded. Payal came at six, grinning, and ate first. 'You changed it for me?' 'Obviously.'

qa.q: Why couldn't Payal eat at the party at seven?
qa.a: It was Paryushan and her family was fasting, so she couldn't eat after sunset.

qa.q: Why did Indu stop herself from saying 'Just once won't matter'?
qa.a: She remembered how respectfully Payal had asked about Christmas and the crib, and wanted to show the same respect back.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Moving the cake cutting before sunset kept Payal included without asking her to break her family's practice.

qa.q: How might Payal have felt when she learned Indu changed the time?
qa.a: She would likely feel respected and cared for, and happy she could fully join the birthday. 🙏

grounding: Shows a child respecting a friend's faith practice under time pressure.

passage: Kamal had never been to a Ganesh pandal before. His classmate Rukmini's colony in Andheri had set one up under a tent of marigolds, and she'd dragged him along after school. The drums were so loud his chest buzzed. He stood near the back, unsure. Could he go in? Should he take off his sneakers? He watched others leave their shoes at the side and did the same. 'Why does Ganpati have a mouse?' he whispered. Rukmini explained, and he listened carefully. Aunties were making rangoli, and one handed him the orange powder. He drew a careful star. On the way home, he asked Rukmini, 'Will you come to our house for Eid? Ammi makes sheer khurma.' 'Obviously!'

qa.q: What did Kamal draw with the orange powder?
qa.a: He drew a careful star in the rangoli.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling as he stood near the back of the pandal?
qa.a: He felt unsure and a bit nervous, not knowing the customs and not wanting to do something wrong.

qa.q: How did Kamal show respect at a festival that wasn't his own?
qa.a: He watched how others behaved, followed along, asked questions quietly and joined in with the rangoli.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see Kamal's invitation to Eid?
qa.a: She would likely feel happy that sharing her festival led to him wanting to share his.

grounding: Shows a child learning about and respecting a friend's festival different from his own.

passage: Sunday: At bedtime, after Rashmi lit the small lamp by the photo of Ajji, she said, 'Let's say three good things from today, Jeevan.' He was eight and grumpy after losing at carrom. 'Nothing was good.' She just said hers and switched off the light. Thursday: The lamp flickered again. Jeevan sat with his knees pulled up, eyes closed for a moment the way Amma did. 'Okay. One: Ma'am let me feed the class fish. That's all.' Rashmi smiled in the dark. Next Tuesday: Rashmi was tired and forgot. Jeevan tugged her sleeve. 'Amma, lamp first. Then my three. I've got four today, actually.' He counted them on his fingers, slowly, before falling asleep.

qa.q: What did Jeevan say was his one good thing on Thursday?
qa.a: His teacher let him feed the class fish.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan say 'Nothing was good' on Sunday?
qa.a: He was grumpy after losing at carrom, so he didn't feel like finding anything good in his day.

qa.q: What made Rashmi's way of starting the habit work?
qa.a: She didn't force him; she simply kept doing it herself each night so he could join when ready.

qa.q: How might Rashmi have felt when Jeevan reminded her on Tuesday?
qa.a: She was probably touched and pleased that the small ritual had become his own. 🤍

grounding: Shows a child gradually taking part in a nightly lamp ritual and gratitude practice.

passage: Vaibhav, you think sitting quietly is punishment, no? I thought the same when I was ten. Every morning my grandfather sat by the river near our town before his puja, and one day he made me come. 'Just sit. Say nothing. Listen,' he said. I fidgeted so much! I counted ants. I sighed loudly. He didn't scold, just kept sitting. After some days I began to hear things: the washerman's slap-slap on stones, a kingfisher diving, my own breath. Then he said, 'Now think of one thing you're thankful for.' I said, 'Mangoes.' He laughed so much. But every morning after that I had one thing. Try with me tomorrow, before school. Only five minutes.

qa.q: What sounds did the narrator begin to hear by the river?
qa.a: The washerman's slapping on stones, a kingfisher diving and the narrator's own breath.

qa.q: How was the narrator feeling during the first days of sitting by the river?
qa.a: Restless and bored; the narrator fidgeted, counted ants and sighed loudly.

qa.q: What worked in the grandfather's way of teaching silence?
qa.a: He kept sitting calmly without scolding and then added a simple gratitude question once the child had settled.

qa.q: Why might Vaibhav find it easier to try with the narrator than alone?
qa.a: Hearing that the narrator was also restless at that age makes it feel less like punishment and more like something shared.

grounding: An elder recalls learning a short silence and gratitude practice as a child alongside a family ritual.

passage: The summer camp at the Rajkot community centre had a new room every day. Himani, eleven, tried everything: Monday she yawned through chess, Tuesday she tripped over her feet in dance, Wednesday the coding class made her head spin. On Thursday it was pottery. She pressed her thumbs into cold clay, and the wheel began to turn. The room noise faded. When Pallavi didi, the camp volunteer, rang the lunch bell, Himani didn't move. 'Himani? Lunch!' 'Two minutes. The side keeps flopping.' Twenty minutes later, her bowl was lopsided and her arms were grey to the elbow. 'You missed lunch,' Pallavi didi said. Himani looked surprised. 'Already? Can I come back tomorrow?'

qa.q: On which day did Himani try pottery?
qa.a: She tried pottery on Thursday.

qa.q: What does Himani not hearing the lunch bell suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests she was completely absorbed in the pottery, more than in any other activity she tried.

qa.q: How could Pallavi didi support what she noticed?
qa.a: She could tell Himani's family about her focus on clay and help her find more chances to try pottery.

qa.q: What would change if the camp had offered only one activity, like chess?
qa.a: Himani might never have discovered pottery and might have thought she wasn't good at anything.

grounding: Shows a child trying many activities and noticing what absorbs her attention.

passage: I'm Zubin, and Ritu sits next to me in class six. This year she's joined everything. In June it was karate; she quit after two weeks. In July she said she'd learn the keyboard, and she did practise a few times. But here's what I keep noticing: whatever class it is, the back of her notebook fills up with comics. Little people with big heads, arguing about lunch. In the maths period she draws. In the bus she draws. Last week our teacher took the notebook, and I thought Ritu would cry. Instead Ma'am laughed and said, 'Make one for the school magazine.' Ritu hasn't talked about karate since. I don't know if she'll become an artist. But she never stops.

qa.q: What does Ritu draw at the back of her notebook?
qa.a: Comics of little people with big heads arguing about lunch.

qa.q: What might Ritu have been feeling when the teacher took her notebook?
qa.a: She was probably scared of being in trouble, which is why Zubin thought she would cry.

qa.q: How could Ritu's family help her explore this interest?
qa.a: They could give her time and paper for comics while still letting her try other activities.

qa.q: Why might Zubin notice Ritu's drawing more than her karate?
qa.a: He sees her drawing everywhere, all the time, while the other activities came and went.

grounding: An observer notices a classmate trying many hobbies and returning again and again to one.

passage: Nandini, come here and close that tap first. Good. Now, when I was your age in Bikaner, water came in a tanker twice a week. My mother kept every drop in brass pots. We bathed with one bucket, and the bath water went to the tulsi and the neem. Dishwater went to the chillies. Once I spilt a whole pot playing, and I cried, because I knew what it meant. So I became the water guard of our house. I scolded my brothers if they let the tap drip at the neighbour's. Here the water comes from a pipe, so you forget. But it doesn't grow in the pipe, beta. Shall we put a mug under the RO waste tomorrow, for mopping?

qa.q: How often did water come to the narrator's childhood home in Bikaner?
qa.a: It came in a tanker twice a week.

qa.q: Why did the narrator cry as a child after spilling a pot?
qa.a: The narrator understood how precious that water was for the family and felt guilty for wasting it.

qa.q: What small step does the narrator suggest to Nandini?
qa.a: Putting a mug under the RO waste pipe so the water can be used for mopping.

qa.q: How might Nandini see water differently after this story?
qa.a: She might start noticing running taps and realise water isn't endless just because it comes easily.

grounding: An elder recalls childhood water-saving habits and passes a small daily habit on to a child.

passage: That May, the building's water came for only one hour each morning, and Yash, eleven, was put in charge of making it last. At six he and his little sister Aadhya filled every bucket and bottle in the flat, yawning. 'Rules,' Yash announced, writing on the fridge. 'Tap off while brushing. One mug of water for washing hands, not running water. Vegetable water goes to the plants.' Aadhya pointed at the ceiling fan whirring in the empty room. 'That's electricity, not water.' 'Still wasting,' said Yash, and switched it off. By the fourth day, two buckets were left over. Papa noticed. 'Did we get extra water?' 'No,' said Aadhya proudly. 'Yash made rules.'

qa.q: How long did the building get water each morning?
qa.a: Only one hour each morning.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel when Papa asked about extra water?
qa.a: She felt proud of the rules and of the buckets they had saved together.

qa.q: Which of Yash's rules could any family try?
qa.a: Turning the tap off while brushing, using a mug for handwashing and giving vegetable water to plants.

qa.q: What would change if the water came all day again?
qa.a: Yash and Aadhya might slip back into careless habits unless they kept the rules going anyway.

grounding: Shows a child saving water and energy at home under a water shortage.

passage: Friday: Madhav, ten, came home to find his clay volcano squashed. Shankar, six, stood beside it with guilty fingers. 'You RUIN everything!' Madhav yelled, and Shankar wailed. Thatha watched from his chair and said nothing. Sunday: Thatha called Madhav to the terrace with a paper kite. 'When your father was small, he broke my radio,' he said, tying the string. 'I shouted at him. He didn't touch anything of mine for a year. I missed him.' Madhav was quiet. Wednesday: Shankar crept up to the terrace to watch. Madhav held out the string. 'Hold here. Don't pull too hard.' The kite dipped and rose. Shankar squealed. Thatha smiled from the doorway.

qa.q: What did Madhav's father break when he was small?
qa.a: He broke Thatha's radio.

qa.q: Why do you think Madhav went quiet after Thatha's story?
qa.a: He was probably realising that shouting at Shankar might push his little brother away, as it had in Thatha's story.

qa.q: What did Thatha do that helped without lecturing?
qa.a: He shared a memory about his own mistake and let Madhav reach his own conclusion.

qa.q: How might Shankar see Madhav after the kite day?
qa.a: He might start trusting his big brother again and want to learn more from him. 😊

grounding: Shows sibling rivalry easing as a child learns from his grandfather and cares for his younger brother.

passage: Manjula, my darling, you're angry with your sister over a hair clip? Let me tell you a secret. When I was ten, I had a red ribbon, a gift from my uncle in Bombay, and my little sister Kamu took it for a wedding without asking. I pulled her hair so hard she cried. My Paati sat me down, not angry, and said, 'Devika, you are the elder. Your sister copies you because she wants to be you.' I didn't understand then. Afterwards, I lent Kamu the ribbon for her school day, and she walked like a queen. We braided each other's hair for fifty years. Now, go and see what your sister wants, and why.

qa.q: Where did the red ribbon come from?
qa.a: It was a gift from young Devika's uncle in Bombay.

qa.q: What did Devika's Paati think Kamu was feeling when she took the ribbon?
qa.a: She thought Kamu admired her elder sister and wanted to be like her.

qa.q: What does Devika suggest Manjula do about the hair clip?
qa.a: To go to her sister and find out what she wants and why, instead of just staying angry.

qa.q: How might Kamu have felt walking to school with the ribbon?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and loved, like a queen, because her big sister chose to share. 🤍

grounding: A grandmother recalls sibling rivalry and a lesson from her own grandmother about caring for a younger sibling.

passage: Three weeks before his Class 12 boards, Vikas stuck a timetable above his desk in their small Nagpur flat: physics in the mornings, chemistry after lunch, maths problems at night, and every Sunday afternoon a full mock paper with a timer. The hardest part wasn't the syllabus. It was his phone. Every buzz pulled him out of a derivation. So he started leaving it on the kitchen shelf with Aai while he studied, fifty minutes at a time, then a ten-minute break on the balcony. When Deepak called to go for chai at nine, Vikas hesitated. 'Saturday, after the mock,' he said. On the day of the physics paper his hands shook, so he did what he'd practised: read the whole paper, circled the easy questions and started there.

qa.q: Where did Vikas leave his phone while studying?
qa.a: On the kitchen shelf with Aai.

qa.q: What might Vikas have been feeling when Deepak called?
qa.a: He was tempted to go and a bit torn, since he wanted to see his friend but also wanted to protect his study time.

qa.q: Which part of Vikas's exam strategy could help a nervous student most?
qa.a: Reading the whole paper first and starting with the easy questions, which builds calm and momentum.

qa.q: How might Deepak see the delayed chai plan?
qa.a: He might be disappointed at first but likely understands and respects his friend's focus before boards.

grounding: Shows a teenager planning revision, resisting distraction and using a strategy in a high-stakes exam.

passage: 'Minakshi, it's eleven. Why are all the chemistry books open at once?' Bhavna mausi stood at the door. 'Because the exam is tomorrow and I don't know anything!' 'You studied all week.' 'But I keep forgetting organic.' Mausi sat on the bed. 'Okay. What's the paper pattern?' 'Three sections. Forty-five minutes each, roughly.' 'Which section is your strongest?' 'Physical chem. Numericals.' 'So start there tomorrow?' Minakshi blinked. 'I always go in order.' 'Who said you have to?' 'Nobody, I guess.' 'And tonight?' 'Just the organic reactions list. Once. Then sleep.' 'Phone?' Minakshi sighed and handed it over. 'Take it. And maybe a hug?' Mausi laughed and gave her one.

qa.q: Which section of chemistry did Minakshi say was her strongest?
qa.a: Physical chemistry, the numericals.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling when all her books were open at once?
qa.a: She was panicking and overwhelmed, fearing she didn't know anything before the exam.

qa.q: How did Mausi help Minakshi build an exam strategy?
qa.a: She asked questions that led Minakshi to start with her strongest section and to do one light revision before sleeping.

qa.q: What would change if Mausi had told Minakshi to stay up all night revising?
qa.a: Minakshi would likely be more exhausted and anxious in the exam and remember less.

grounding: Shows a teenager calming exam panic, planning final revision and choosing a strategy for a high-stakes test.

passage:
Dear Kiran di,
You told me to write after the inter-school debate, so here goes. We lost the semi-final. My motion was 'Homework should be banned in school', and I was FOR it. I had strong feelings but, honestly, weak evidence. I said 'homework causes stress' and the other side asked, 'Where's your source?' I froze.
For the final round, I changed my prep. I found two studies our librarian helped me with, and I wrote the best argument AGAINST me on a card and practised answering it fairly: yes, some practice at home helps with maths, but not three hours a night. The judge wrote 'fair rebuttal' on my sheet! Still lost, but I felt like a real debater.
Miss your tips,
Baljeet

qa.q: What was the motion Baljeet debated?
qa.a: 'Homework should be banned in school', and he argued for it.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when the other side asked for his source?
qa.a: He froze, caught out because he had strong feelings but weak evidence.

qa.q: What did Baljeet change that made his argument stronger?
qa.a: He found real studies and prepared a fair answer to the best argument against him.

qa.q: How might Kiran di react to this letter?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud that Baljeet learned from losing and used her advice to improve.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning to build claims on evidence and answer counter-arguments fairly.

passage: So you want to know how I got into debating? Honestly, by losing badly. Class nine, the topic was whether school uniforms should be scrapped. I'm Lavanya, by the way, I'm fifteen. I went up with pure fire: 'Uniforms kill creativity!' Big applause from my friends. Then Sarika from the other school stood up, totally calm. She said, 'That's a fair worry. But here's a survey from our district where students said uniforms reduce teasing about clothes.' She actually repeated my point before answering it! I had nothing to say back. I was so annoyed with myself on the bus home. Now before every debate I write, claim, evidence, and what the other side will say. And I try to answer the way Sarika did.

qa.q: What was the debate topic in class nine?
qa.a: Whether school uniforms should be scrapped.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel on the bus home?
qa.a: She was annoyed with herself for having only passion and no evidence or answer to Sarika's point.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's new preparation method do well?
qa.a: It makes her back each claim with evidence and plan a fair response to the other side before she speaks.

qa.q: How might Sarika have seen Lavanya's fiery speech?
qa.a: She probably respected the worry behind it, which is why she repeated it fairly before answering with evidence.

grounding: A teenager recalls learning to support claims with evidence and to answer counter-arguments fairly.

passage:
Damini: omg look at this ad 😍 'Students who joined our coaching improved scores by 40% on average!!'
Damini: should I tell Papa?
Tanvir: 40% of what though 🤔
Damini: of their marks??
Tanvir: If someone had 20/100 and went to 28, that's 40% up. Still failing.
Damini: hmm
Tanvir: also how many students? 5? 500?
Damini: it doesn't say
Tanvir: and did the ones who improved maybe just start studying more? Or did they only count the kids who stayed?
Damini: ugh you ruin everything
Damini: ok but fair
Tanvir: ask them for the real numbers. If they won't show, that says something
Damini: fine. writing an email. you're checking it
Tanvir: 👍

qa.q: By how much did the ad claim scores improved?
qa.a: It claimed scores improved by 40% on average.

qa.q: What does Damini's 'ugh you ruin everything' followed by 'ok but fair' suggest she felt?
qa.a: She was disappointed to lose her excitement about the ad but accepted that Tanvir's questions made sense.

qa.q: What questions could anyone ask when an ad uses percentages?
qa.a: Percent of what starting number, how many people were counted, and whether something else might explain the change.

qa.q: How might a coaching centre see a student asking for the real numbers?
qa.a: An honest centre would share them; one that avoids answering might be hiding weak results.

grounding: A teen chat shows questioning an average and a percentage claim instead of being fooled by numbers.

passage: The forward reached every phone in the kasba on the same afternoon: 'Thefts up 200% this year! Buy strong locks now!' By evening a man with a van of padlocks had parked near the bus stand. Irfan, fifteen, watched his sister Pooja reach for her savings tin. 'Wait,' he said. 'Two hundred percent of what?' He walked to the police chowki notice board, where the monthly list was pinned, and counted. Last year, one theft. This year, three. 'It's three. Out of the whole kasba. That's the two hundred percent.' Pooja frowned. 'So it's nothing?' 'Not nothing. Lock the gate at night, sure. But nobody needs to panic-buy from that van.' She put the tin back.

qa.q: How many thefts did Irfan count for this year on the notice board?
qa.a: He counted three thefts this year, compared with one last year.

qa.q: Why did Irfan tell Pooja to wait before buying a lock?
qa.a: He suspected the big percentage was hiding a small number and that the seller was using fear to make sales.

qa.q: Which of Irfan's steps would help anyone facing a scary statistic?
qa.a: He checked the real numbers at the source and explained them calmly without dismissing the risk completely.

qa.q: How might the lock seller see Irfan's questions?
qa.a: He might be annoyed, because his sales depend on people being scared by the big percentage.

grounding: A rural teen checks a scary percentage against real counts instead of being fooled by numbers.

passage: So Suraj, you know Rakesh sir, the one who's always on those study videos? He said students who study with music score higher. Everyone in our class started repeating it. Even my cousin put on headphones while doing trigonometry. I got curious and found the survey he quoted. It was twenty students from one coaching centre. Twenty! And they just asked them if they liked music and what their marks were. It didn't test anything. Maybe kids who can afford their own quiet room with speakers also have tutors. That's correlation, not causation, right? I'm not saying music is bad. I'm saying a famous person repeating something ten times doesn't make it evidence. Now I ask: how big was the study, and what did they actually measure?

qa.q: How many students were in the survey Rakesh sir quoted?
qa.a: Twenty students from one coaching centre.

qa.q: What made the narrator curious enough to look up the survey?
qa.a: Everyone was repeating the claim, even the narrator's cousin, and the narrator wanted to know if it was really true.

qa.q: What questions does the narrator now use to judge a claim?
qa.a: How big the study was and what it actually measured, rather than trusting who said it.

qa.q: How might the narrator's classmates react to these findings?
qa.a: Some might feel silly for copying the idea, while others might defend the famous teacher out of habit.

grounding: A teen explains judging a claim by the quality of evidence and spotting correlation versus causation, not authority.

passage: I'm Ganga, Tushar's older sister. For the science fair, he wanted to test whether plants grow better with music, because his friend's uncle swore by it and everyone in the building repeated it. First he put a pot beside the radio on the sunny windowsill and another in the corner. The windowsill plant grew taller. He was thrilled. Then he stopped and stared at them for ages. I don't know what went through his head. The next day he moved both plants to the same windowsill, same water, same soil, and played music to only one. Three weeks later they were almost the same height. He wrote on his chart: 'Sunlight, not songs?' His teacher gave him a special mention.

qa.q: Where did Tushar first place the plant with the radio?
qa.a: On the sunny windowsill.

qa.q: What might Tushar have been thinking as he stared at the plants for ages?
qa.a: He may have realised the windowsill plant also had more sunlight, so music might not be the cause, though Ganga isn't sure.

qa.q: Why was Tushar's second experiment better than the first?
qa.a: He kept sunlight, water and soil the same so only the music differed, which gave fairer evidence.

qa.q: How might the friend's uncle respond to Tushar's result?
qa.a: He might be surprised or unwilling to believe it, since he had repeated the claim with such confidence.

grounding: An observer describes a teen testing a repeated claim and separating correlation from cause.
